questions.q: What cryptographic approach does the FIDO2/WebAuthn standard use for authentication?
options: A static API key embedded in the login request
A six-digit code regenerated every 30 seconds from a shared secret
A shared secret password that is hashed before being sent to the server
Public-key cryptography, where a private key never leaves the device and a public key is stored by the site
questions.explain: FIDO2 uses a device-generated key pair: the private key stays on the device, and the public key is what the site stores.

questions.q: What is 'origin binding' in FIDO2, and why does it matter?
options: The credential can be freely copied and used on any website without restriction
The credential is cryptographically tied to the exact domain it was created for, so it refuses to work on a phishing lookalike page
The credential only works on the device where it was first created, and nowhere else ever
The credential expires automatically after 30 days regardless of use
questions.explain: A FIDO2 credential checks that the page's origin matches the one it was registered for, which is what makes it phishing-resistant.

questions.q: What is a passkey, as described in this lesson?
options: The consumer-friendly implementation of FIDO2, with the private key synced across a user's devices via a platform provider
A legacy term for a traditional memorized password
A physical hardware token that must be plugged in for every single login
A one-time code sent by SMS to verify identity
questions.explain: Passkeys package FIDO2 for everyday use, syncing the credential across devices through providers like Apple, Google, or Microsoft.

questions.q: What is an MFA-fatigue, or 'push-bombing,' attack?
options: A technique for cracking FIDO2 private keys through repeated login attempts
A method attackers use to intercept SMS codes via SIM swapping
A denial-of-service attack against an identity provider's servers
Spamming a user with repeated push-approval requests until they tap 'approve' out of confusion or fatigue
questions.explain: Push-bombing exploits the human decision point in push-based MFA by firing repeated requests until one gets approved by mistake.

questions.q: Why are FIDO2 and passkeys considered stronger than SMS- or push-based MFA?
options: They require no device of any kind to use
They are immune to all forms of account compromise under every circumstance
They remove the human decision point entirely and are bound to the real site's origin, so there's nothing to read aloud, approve under pressure, or use on a lookalike page
They replace the need for any identity provider entirely
questions.explain: Because the check is automatic and origin-bound, there's no code to intercept and no push approval a user can be socially engineered into granting.
